extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy / ethics (Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative criteria for moral qualities (jocularity, shame, self-control) and for Justice (distributive, corrective, reciprocity, money as measure). The passage lays out definitions, examples, and contrasts (excess/defect/mean) that serve as standards for judging character and social transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration vs Reserve in speech and character
rubrics_metrics.description: Excess and extreme deficiency both partake of the nature of Exaggeration; Reserve in moderation gives an impression of refinement; Exaggerator is opposed to the Truthful Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reserve moderately—too much plainness or too much reserve both verge on exaggeration; the mean produces refinement. Example: extreme plainness of dress (Lacedaemonians) illustrates excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buffoon (exceeding in the ridiculous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who exceed in the ridiculous are judged Buffoons and Vulgar, catching at comic effect in any way and at any cost, aiming at raising laughter rather than saying what is seemly or avoiding to pain the object of their wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: seeking laughter by any means, sparing neither self nor others, using obscene or gratuitous remarks. Buffoonery confuses easy pleasantry with vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clownish / Stern (defect in jocularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who refuse to make a joke and are displeased with joking are thought Clownish and Stern; they contribute nothing jocose of their own and are 'savage' with those who do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: total abstention from appropriate lightness; failure to participate in socially fitting pastime harms ease of intercourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity in good taste (Tact / Easy Pleasantry)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state: being jocular in good taste (a kind of ease of movement); a man of Tact says and listens to such things as are fit for a good man and gentleman to say and hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria: say what is becoming to a gentleman; avoid causing pain to the object of wit; sometimes give pleasure. Distinguish gentlemanly jocularity (innuendo, refinement) from vulgar obscene talk. A refined person is 'a law to himself'—moderation and sensitivity are required. Some scurrility is legally forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decency differences by education and genre (Old vs New Comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jocularity of a gentleman differs from that of the vulgar and of the educated from the uneducated; Old Comedy relied on obscene talk, New Comedy on innuendo—this marks a significant difference in decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or producing comedic material, consider audience education and genre conventions; prefer innuendo and restraint for refined taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shame is a feeling, not a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Shame is more like a feeling (a kind of fear of disgrace) than a moral state; it is appropriate to youth as a check on passion, but does not belong to the good man who ought not to do disgraceful things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shame acts on voluntary actions only; it may be 'good' only hypothetically ('if a man should do such things, he would feel Shame'), but virtues are good in themselves. Do not treat Shame as constitutive of moral goodness in adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Control as a mixed state
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-Control is not properly a virtue but a kind of mixed state (briefly noted; fuller treatment deferred).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims about self-control cautiously; it occupies a different category from full virtues and feelings like Shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as a moral state enabling just action and desire
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is a moral state such that, in consequence of it, men have the capacity of doing what is just, actually do it, and wish it; Injustice is the corresponding state for unjust actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition as ground-work: justice concerns dispositions and actions toward others, not merely isolated acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful (legal) acts as just; law aims at common good
rubrics_metrics.description: Violating the law is Unjust and keeping the law Just; laws give directions aiming at the common good of all, the best, or those in power, and lawful actions are in a manner Just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing justice, consider conformity to legitimate law intended to promote social goods; good laws command virtuous actions and forbid vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as the practice of perfect virtue toward one's neighbour
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is in fact perfect Virtue as exercised towards one's neighbour; it is special because it enables practising virtue in relation to others (not merely oneself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate justice by whether the agent can and does extend virtuous conduct into social transactions and relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between co-extensive justice (virtue-wide) and particular justice
rubrics_metrics.description: There is Justice co-extensive with Virtue (practice of virtue in all bearings to others) and Particular Justice (a part of virtue concerned with dealings affecting share/ratio between persons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to separate the general moral excellence (virtue) from the narrower legal/social sense of justice when analyzing cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Justice: Distributive Justice (proportionate share)
rubrics_metrics.description: One species of Particular Justice concerns distributions of honour, wealth, or other divisible goods—this Distributive Just is proportionate: the Just is a certain proportionable thing (e.g., A:B::C:D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributive justice requires preserving equality of ratios (geometrical/proportional equality) among persons and things; different political groups may propose different 'rates' (virtue, wealth, birth) for distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Justice: Corrective Justice (restoring arithmetical equality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corrective justice concerns transactions between persons (voluntary and involuntary) and is an arithmetical equalizing: the judge seeks to restore equality by taking from the greater and adding to the less—the mean between loss and gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In disputes, aim for arithmetic restoration: estimate loss and gain, apply penalty to remove unjust excess. This form of justice treats parties as previously equal for adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs Involuntary transactions (jurisdiction of corrective justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary transactions: selling, buying, use, bail, borrowing, deposit, hiring. Involuntary: secrecy crimes (theft, adultery, poisoning, pimping, kidnapping slaves, assassination, false witness) and open violence (insult, bonds, death, plundering, maiming, foul language, slander).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification to decide how to judge and remedy wrongdoing: voluntary exchanges governed by contract-like rules; involuntary harms call for corrective/legal redress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge as middle-man: role to attain the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge (mesitidos/middle-man) is meant to be the personification of the Just whose office is to make things equal—take from the greater part its excess and add to the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudication aims at the mean between extremes; judges should function as impartial restorers of equality rather than partisan rulers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocation must be proportionate, not simple equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple reciprocation ('that which reciprocates') fails for distributive and corrective justice; reciprocation in exchange must be according to proportion, not exact equality; reciprocity of good fosters social bonds (χάρις).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying reciprocity, account for proportion (quality and quantity) and contextual factors like authority and voluntariness; avoid crude 'tit-for-tat' where inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money and demand as common measure for exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: All things which can be exchanged must be commensurable; money has arisen as a medium and representative of Demand, making things commensurable and equalising them for exchange; price-setting enables exchange at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use money/price as the practical measure to equalize heterogeneous goods in assessments of fairness in exchange; remember purchasing power can vary (depreciation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural vs Conventional Justice; domestic vs social justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Just is natural (same everywhere), some conventional (dependent on enactment); domestic justice (master/father and child/slave) differs from social justice because some things are 'one's own' and not subject to the same possibility of injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between natural moral requirements and legally/conventionally imposed rules; adjust standards depending on relational context (domestic, political, social).

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice as mean aiming to produce the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: Just acting is a mean between acting unjustly and being acted unjustly towards (the former equivalent to having more, the latter to having less); Justice aims at producing proportionate equality, whereas Injustice occupies the extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating conduct, consider whether actions tend to create proportionate outcomes (mean) or to create excess/defect (injustice).
